hero.headline.text: Which part does the answer rely on?

hero.highlight.text: Remove one part at a time and see.

hero.takeaway.text: The context of one request is made of the system prompt, the earlier conversation, the tool call and tool result, and this turn's question. Remove one part, ask the same question again, and you can see which part the answer depends on. The tool call and the tool result can only be removed together.

concepts.01-parts.title.text: The four parts of the context

concepts.01-parts.description.text: The system prompt, the earlier conversation, the tool call and tool result, and this turn's question are put together in a fixed order as this request's messages.

concepts.02-ablation.title.text: Remove one part at a time

concepts.02-ablation.description.text: Every other message stays word for word the same, with just one part missing. Whatever the answer lacks can then be attributed to that part.

concepts.03-pair.title.text: A call and its result come as a pair

concepts.03-pair.description.text: An assistant message with tool_calls must be followed immediately by a tool message with the same call id.

concepts.04-check.description.text: validate_tool_history checks the pairing first. A history that is not valid is not sent.

section-1.paragraphs.0.text: All the model can use when it answers is what is in this one request, so first work out what this request contains. {{lesson:multi-turn-history}} showed that the model does not remember the previous turn and the program has to resend the history. In {{lesson:dependent-calls}}, tool results were also put back into the history as messages, so the next request could see them. This lesson takes the context of one request apart to see which parts it has and which part each answer relies on.

section-1.paragraphs.1.text: This lesson's full context is five messages in four parts. System prompt: one system message, which says to answer only from this request's messages and to end with a separate line starting "Basis:". Earlier conversation: one user message, "This week I can only review on Thursday evening. First, look up the latest exercise for s-1042.". Tool call and tool result: one assistant message with tool_calls, plus one tool message holding a score of 73 and a passing line of 60. This turn's question: one user message, "Did I pass that exercise? Which day should I review this week?".

section-1.paragraphs.2.text: The four parts have different jobs. The system prompt provides no facts; it only sets how to answer. The earlier conversation brings in what the user said. The tool result brings in facts the program looked up. This turn's question says what to answer now. The question needs two pieces of information to be answered fully: the score is only in the tool result, and the review day is only in the earlier conversation. This is deliberate. Each piece of information sits in one place only, so when it shows up in the answer, you can tie it to that part.

section-1.paragraphs.3.text: An analogy: it is like handing a new colleague a folder holding the task description, the earlier correspondence, the data that was looked up, and today's question. He can only work from what is in the folder. However smart he is, he does not know what is not in it. Also note that this lesson's request has no `tools` field: the model can see the earlier call and its result, but this time there is no tool it can call.

section-2.title.text: Remove one part at a time

section-2.paragraphs.0.text: To find out which part an answer relies on, leave everything else word for word the same, remove one part at a time, and see what the answer lacks. This is called ablation. It follows the same rule as the pairs in {{lesson:prompt-experiments}}: change one thing at a time. If you remove two parts at once and the answer lacks something, you cannot tell which part to blame.

section-2.paragraphs.1.text: One run of this lesson prepares five context variants: the full context; without the system prompt; without the earlier conversation; without the tool call and result; and without only the tool result, keeping the call. All five variants ask the same question, with temperature 0. assemble builds the messages in a fixed order and skips only the part this variant removes. Every message that stays keeps its position and its text.

section-2.paragraphs.2.text: The comparison is straightforward. Without the tool call and result, does the answer still contain 73? Without the earlier conversation, does it still mention Thursday? Without the system prompt, does it still write the "Basis:" line? If the answer lacks the matching information once a part is removed, that shows this answer used that part. The reverse does not hold: if the answer does not change after removal, you cannot conclude that the part was useless. The model may simply have a habit of writing that way.

section-2.paragraphs.3.text: These five messages are samples assembled by the runner. The assistant message with tool_calls is written by the runner and was not proposed by the model. The score in the tool message comes from a real execution of lookup_score in this run, and the origin of that call in the events is course_program. The runner hard-codes this call so that the differences among the five variants come only from the removed part. If the model proposed the call itself each time, the proposals could differ, which would add a variable.

deep-dive-ablation-book.title.text: A bigger ablation: what happens to an agent when a part is missing

deep-dive-ablation-book.summary.text: *Understanding AI Agents in Depth* (深入理解 AI Agent) ran the same kind of ablation on a complete agent. Its conclusion is that when information is missing, the agent often does not raise an error but gives an answer that looks fine.

deep-dive-ablation-book.paragraphs.0.text: At the start, where it describes what an agent is made of, *Understanding AI Agents in Depth* splits the context of one request into five parts: system prompt, tool definitions, user messages, model replies, and tool execution results. Compared with this lesson's split, it adds tool definitions. A tool definition is not a message but the top-level `tools` field of the request. Its user messages and model replies together roughly correspond to this lesson's earlier conversation and this turn's question. The two splits describe the same request.

deep-dive-ablation-book.paragraphs.1.text: The book's experiment runs on an agent that calls tools many times. One variant keeps everything, and four other variants each remove one part: the tool definitions, the tool execution results, the thinking process in the model replies, and the earlier history messages. The system prompt did not take part. The book's reason is that without it the agent does not even have a basic role. This lesson does the reverse and removes it, because this lesson's system prompt only sets how to answer, so the answers stay comparable without it. According to the book's records: with the tool definitions removed, the model cannot call tools, yet still writes a neatly formatted, confident answer, with numbers coming from what the model learned in training. With the tool execution results removed, the agent cannot see what happened, retries over and over, and keeps going until it hits the round limit.

deep-dive-ablation-book.paragraphs.2.text: The book draws two points from this. First, "gave an answer" does not mean "completed the task": when the context lacks something, the typical failure is not an error but an answer with no visible flaw. Second, the parts are not equally important. The book's yardstick is whether the information can be rebuilt from elsewhere. The thinking process records "why it did this", and when it can be reconstructed from the tool results, removing it costs almost nothing. The tool results record "what happened outside", and once removed they cannot be recovered. With a different model, the ablation conclusions may also differ. These are the book's records and this lesson did not reproduce them. This lesson takes only the smallest step: the same question, five context variants, one request each.

deep-dive-ablation-book.paragraphs.3.text: In Claude Code you can see these parts directly. Run `/context` during a session and it shows by category how much of the current context each takes, including which `CLAUDE.md` instruction files were loaded. The official documentation also says which role the instruction files go in: the content of `CLAUDE.md` is delivered as a user message after the system prompt, not as part of the system prompt. Compared with this lesson, `/context` tells you how big each part is, but not which part the answer used. To know that, you still have to remove a part and ask again, as this lesson does. Check the official documentation for the exact display.

predict-request-count.prompt.text: Before you run "Student s-1042: five context variants compared" in the experiment, predict: one run prepares five context variants, so how many model calls (request events) will this run make in total?

mq-missing-score.missing-score.prompt.text: Suppose the answer in the "Remove the tool call and result" variant does not mention the score of 73. What is the most direct explanation?

mq-missing-score.missing-score.a.text.text: This request has no tool result, so the model cannot get the score

mq-missing-score.missing-score.a.feedbac.text: Correct. The score is only in that tool message, and this request no longer has it.

mq-missing-score.missing-score.b.text.text: The model forgot the score it looked up in the previous request

mq-missing-score.missing-score.b.feedbac.text: Not quite. The model never remembered the previous request, so there is nothing to forget. It only sees the messages in this request.

mq-missing-score.missing-score.c.text.text: The system prompt does not let it mention the score

mq-missing-score.missing-score.c.feedbac.text: Not quite. This variant keeps the system prompt and the rule has not changed. Only the tool call and result changed.

mq-missing-score.missing-score.explanati.text: Remove one part at a time, and the information the answer lacks can be tied to the part that was removed.

section-3.title.text: Tool calls and tool results must come as a pair

section-3.paragraphs.0.text: A tool call and its result must be paired one to one by call id. Rules like this, which fix the order and pairing of messages, are called the message protocol. The tool call sits in the tool_calls of an assistant message, and each item has an id. The id of this lesson's call is lookup_score_1. It must be followed immediately by a message whose role is tool and whose tool_call_id is also lookup_score_1, and its content is the result of that call.

section-3.paragraphs.1.text: Why rely on an id and not just on order? In {{lesson:dependent-calls}}, the model proposed two calls in the same round, the runner executed them one by one, and sent back two tool messages. If you pair by order alone, once the two results are in the wrong order, the time result could be taken as the addition result. With an id, each result states which call it answers, like a courier tracking number: even if the parcels get shuffled, you can still tell whose is whose.

section-3.paragraphs.2.text: Spelled out in full, there are four rules: a call id cannot be empty or duplicated; while a call is still waiting for its result, the next message can only be a tool message; each tool message must answer a call that is still waiting; and when the messages end, no call may still be without a result. This lesson's validate_tool_history checks exactly these four, one by one.

section-3.paragraphs.3.text: So the third part is a pair of messages, and it can only be removed as a whole. The "Remove the tool call and result" variant does exactly that: three messages remain, and the order is still valid. Providers enforce rules like this with different strictness, so follow each provider's documentation. This lesson enforces the rule on its own side first.

section-4.title.text: What if only the tool result is removed

section-4.paragraphs.0.text: If you remove only the tool result and keep the call, the history violates the message protocol, and this lesson stops it before sending. The messages of variant 5 are: system, the earlier conversation, an assistant message with the call lookup_score_1, and this turn's question. The assistant proposed a call, but a user message follows directly, so the call never gets its result.

section-4.paragraphs.1.text: validate_tool_history walks down the messages. When it reads the assistant message, it records lookup_score_1 in outstanding, meaning "proposed, still waiting for a result". When it reads the next user message, outstanding is not empty, so it raises "A tool call must be followed by its tool message first.". The runner catches this error, records a lesson.context with rejected, and moves on to the next variant without sending a request. So only four of the five variants produce request events.

section-4.paragraphs.2.text: Why not just send it and see? First, it saves one request. Second, attribution stays clear: if the provider returns an error, you might think "information is missing and the model cannot answer", when in fact the request format is invalid. Third, providers do not react consistently: some reject it outright and some accept it as is. {{lesson:context-budget}} will deliberately send a history that violates the message protocol (a lone tool result right after system) unchanged to see how the provider handles it.

section-4.paragraphs.3.text: The other way around, removing only the call and keeping the tool message, is invalid too: the id this tool message answers is not in outstanding, and the check raises "Orphaned or duplicate tool message.". This lesson does not include that variant, but you can find the matching line in the Code scene.

deep-dive-chat-template.title.text: On the provider's side: how messages become a string of tokens

deep-dive-chat-template.summary.text: The model does not read a JSON list. It reads one long string of tokens laid out by a chat template, and role markers tell it who said each part.

deep-dive-chat-template.paragraphs.0.text: The messages you send are a JSON list, and the model does not read JSON directly. After receiving the request, the provider joins all the messages into one long text in the format this model was trained on, then cuts it into tokens for the model. This format is called the chat template. The Hugging Face Agents Course gives an example: for the same conversation, SmolLM2 separates each message with special tokens like `<|im_start|>user`, while Llama 3.2 uses a different set of markers.

deep-dive-chat-template.paragraphs.1.text: So "the model remembers the previous turn" is just an illusion of the interface. On every request, the model reads the whole string from the start. Roles are also conveyed by these markers: which part is the system prompt, which is what the user said, which is a tool result. The model learned these markers in training, and it tends to treat a tool result as the output of a program, not as a new request from the user.

deep-dive-chat-template.paragraphs.2.text: This also explains why the message protocol matters. The chat template assumes a call is followed by its result. If the result is missing or misplaced, the resulting text has a shape the model rarely saw in training, so the model may misread it, or the provider may simply reject it. If you send a tool result as a user message, the template treats it as a new sentence from the user. *Understanding AI Agents in Depth* gives a Qwen3 example: when its chat template meets a new user message, it clears the earlier thinking content. A tool result mislabeled as a user message wrongly triggers this cleanup, and reasoning that was half done has to start over. How the template is laid out and which cases get rejected differ between providers, so follow the provider's documentation.

deep-dive-chat-template.paragraphs.3.text: One more thing to be clear about: this platform's request event records the JSON request body sent to the provider. Laying it out as a chat template and cutting it into tokens happen on the provider's side. You cannot see them in the events, and you should not take the messages in request to be the string the model actually reads.

misconception-tool-as-user.claim.text: A tool result is just text. If pairing is a hassle, turn it into a user message and send that. The model can use it just the same.

misconception-tool-as-user.correction.text: The role becomes part of the text the model actually reads. After you change it to a user message, what the model reads is "the user said something else", not "the result of the call just made", and the call id is gone, so it is unclear which call it answers. If you keep the call and change only the result, the protocol check stops it. If you delete the call too and rewrite the result, the check passes, but the model may misunderstand where this information came from and how much weight it carries. To remove a tool interaction, remove the call and the result together as a pair.

mq-blocked.blocked.prompt.text: Why does the "Remove only the tool result" variant have no request event?

mq-blocked.blocked.a.text.text: The pre-send protocol check found a call without a tool result, and the runner did not send a request

mq-blocked.blocked.a.feedback.text: Correct. A history that is not valid is stopped before sending, and the reason is recorded in the rejected field of lesson.context.

mq-blocked.blocked.b.text.text: The provider rejected the request, so nothing was recorded

mq-blocked.blocked.b.feedback.text: Not quite. A request the provider rejects still leaves a request event first. This variant was never sent.

mq-blocked.blocked.c.text.text: This run used up its model calls

mq-blocked.blocked.c.feedback.text: Not quite. It was stopped by the protocol check, which has nothing to do with the call limit. The rejected field holds a protocol problem.

mq-blocked.blocked.explanation.text: Check first, then send: this neither wastes a request nor mistakes a protocol error for the model being unable to answer.

section-5.paragraphs.0.text: Read the result in three layers, ruling things out layer by layer, and look at the answer last. Layer 1: was the request sent, and was it accepted? A variant that was sent has request and response events. A variant that was stopped has only a lesson.context with rejected. A variant the provider rejected has an extra lesson.provider_error.

section-5.paragraphs.1.text: Layer 2: is that part in this request? Expand the messages of the request and count them. The report table also lists the message count for each variant. The full context has 5, without the system prompt or the earlier conversation has 4, and without the tool call and result has 3. This layer rules out the mistake of "thought it was removed, but it was still there".

section-5.paragraphs.2.text: Only layer 3 looks at whether the answer used it. The three report columns "Mentions score", "Mentions review day" and "Has basis line" are a keyword screen: the program only checks whether the answer contains the score, the review day and the word "Basis", and does not understand meaning. An answer that writes "seventy-three" is missed, and one that writes "I can't tell whether it is Thursday" is wrongly counted, so check against the answer's original text.

section-5.paragraphs.3.text: Run it again with s-2077: the tool result becomes 58 points, a fail, and the other messages stay the same. If the full-context answer then says fail as well, its conclusion really came from the tool result, and not from a stock phrase that happened to be right.

mq-screening.screening.prompt.text: Suppose the "Mentions review day" column for the "Remove the earlier conversation" variant shows true. What should you do next?

mq-screening.screening.a.text.text: Read this variant's answer in its original text and see how it mentions the review day

mq-screening.screening.a.feedback.text: Correct. The screen checks only the literal text. The answer may have written "I can't tell whether it is Thursday".

mq-screening.screening.b.text.text: Conclude that the model remembered Thursday

mq-screening.screening.b.feedback.text: Not quite. The model does not keep the previous request. First confirm the messages of this variant do not contain that sentence, then read the answer's original text.

mq-screening.screening.c.text.text: Switch to another model and rerun

mq-screening.screening.c.feedback.text: Not quite. Switching models adds a new variable and cannot explain this screening result.

mq-screening.screening.explanation.text: Look at what is in the request first, then read the answer's original text. The screen is a hint, not a conclusion.

section-6.paragraphs.0.text: One ablation sends several requests. It suits doing a few controlled comparisons while designing the context, and does not suit doing it for every answer. One run of this lesson sends four requests, each carrying nearly the same messages, so the cost is several times that of sending just one.

section-6.paragraphs.1.text: The conclusions hold only for this run and this model. The model still writing the basis line without the system prompt does not show the rule was useless: it may simply write that way by habit, and you need more runs to tell. What ablation can show is "whether that part was in this request and whether the answer used it". It cannot show how the model uses that information internally. In offline test mode the answers are assembled by the test fixture from the message content, and are used only to test the program.

section-6.paragraphs.2.text: This lesson looked at what goes into one request. The next two lessons each ask one question. Should progress, such as how far the task has got and which facts have been checked, also be stuffed into messages? {{lesson:application-state}} puts it into the program's own state. When the context grows too long to fit, which part gets dropped? {{lesson:context-budget}} truncates by budget, and keeps to the message protocol when it truncates.

walkthrough.description.text: Explains step by step how one run assembles five context variants. The code is a simplified illustration. Check the real messages and answers in the event panel.

walkthrough.step-1.body.text: The runner makes one lookup_score call, and the tool result comes from the local score table.

walkthrough.step-2.body.text: One each for the system prompt, the earlier conversation, the call, the result, and this turn's question.

walkthrough.step-3.body.text: Build the messages in a fixed order and skip only the part this variant removes.

walkthrough.step-4.body.text: The variant that removes only the tool result is stopped here and no request is sent.

walkthrough.step-5.body.text: Each of the four valid variants is sent once, and the answers are recorded as they are.

walkthrough.step-6.body.text: Message count, protocol check, original answer text, and the three screening columns side by side.

code-context-parts.n38.text.text: Five variants: each key is a variant's code and each value lists the parts it removes; an empty tuple is the full context. The variant names are in variant_names, one set per run language.

code-context-parts.n42.text.text: The call and result are a pair: take both or neither, and the remaining history is still valid.

code-context-parts.n43.text.text: Deliberately remove only the result and keep the call: this variant violates the message protocol and is used to demonstrate the pre-send check.

code-context-parts.n47.text.text: Each of the five messages has its own key, and the key is the part's name. Ablation skips by key and never changes the content of any message. The message text comes from t, the catalog of the run's language.

code-context-parts.n54.text.text: The earlier conversation: the review day appears only here. If the answer mentions it, this part was used.

code-context-parts.n57.text.text: This assistant message was written by the runner and was not proposed by the model. The call id is the same as in the real execution, so the events and the messages line up.

code-context-parts.n59.text.text: The content is the real return value of this call_tool. The score is only in this message.

code-context-parts.n67.text.text: Build in a fixed order: each variant has only a few messages fewer than the full context, and the position and text of the rest do not change.

code-history-protocol.n70.text.text: The protocol check before sending: it only reads the message list and raises ValueError when it is invalid, and the runner then decides not to send the request. locale only decides the language of the error text.

code-history-protocol.n72.text.text: outstanding holds the ids of calls that were proposed and are still waiting for a result. If it is not empty, a call is waiting for its result.

code-history-protocol.n77.text.text: While a call is waiting for its result, the next message can only be a tool message. Variant 5 is stopped here: this turn's question comes right after the call.

code-history-protocol.n83.text.text: The call id is the only basis for pairing. An empty or duplicate id cannot be matched one to one with a result.

code-history-protocol.n90.text.text: A tool result must answer a call that is still waiting. An orphaned or duplicate tool message is rejected outright.

code-history-protocol.n96.text.text: A call still without a result when the messages end is also invalid.

code-ablation-run.n-texts.text.text: t is the catalog of this run's language: the system prompt, the variant names and the report text all come from it. There is one in Chinese and one in English.

code-ablation-run.n103.text.text: call_tool is run by the runner, records the tool_call and tool_result events, and marks origin as course_program.

code-ablation-run.n107.text.text: The five messages are assembled only once. All five variants pick from this same copy, and the variants differ only in what was removed.

code-ablation-run.n110.text.text: Variants are processed in the order of VARIANTS; the variant that gets stopped comes last. The variant names come from variant_names in the run's language.

code-ablation-run.n115.text.text: Each variant is checked once before sending. A variant that fails the check only has its reason recorded, then the run jumps to the next variant.

code-ablation-run.n117.text.text: A stopped variant is recorded as a lesson.context with rejected, and has no request event.

code-ablation-run.n121.text.text: Variants that pass the check are numbered in send order, and lesson.context and the request that follows share the same round.

code-ablation-run.n123.text.text: _send sends the request with context.complete. If the provider rejects it, it is recorded as lesson.provider_error and not retried.

code-ablation-run.n125.text.text: Assembling the report has nothing to do with this lesson. It lives in _report and the Code scene does not expand it.

code-decision.title.text: Find which part the answer relies on with valid ablation

code-decision.chosen.text: Send five context variants for the same question, each with just one part fewer than the full context. Remove the tool call and tool result as a pair. Before sending, use validate_tool_history to stop the variant that removes only the result.

code-decision.drop-all.title.text: Remove everything and keep only this turn's question

code-decision.drop-all.why_not.text: Three parts are missing at once, so if the answer changes you cannot tell which part did it.

code-decision.drop-any.title.text: Delete any single message, for example only the tool message

code-decision.drop-any.why_not.text: It leaves a call with no result, which violates the message protocol. The provider may reject it outright, and the failure reason becomes a protocol error rather than missing information.

code-decision.model-call.title.text: Let the model propose the tool call itself

code-decision.model-call.why_not.text: The call the model proposes may differ each time, which adds a variable among the five variants. This lesson has the runner write a fixed call and states that honestly in the events.

context-ablation.title.text: Remove one part at a time

context-ablation.hypothesis.text: Same question, same model: whichever part is removed, the answer lacks the information that part provided. Without the tool call and result there is no basis for the score. Without the earlier conversation there is no review day. Without the system prompt the answer is no longer bound by the "Basis:" format. A history with only the tool result removed violates the message protocol and is stopped before sending.

context-ablation.ablate.label.text: Student s-1042: five context variants compared

context-ablation.other-student.label.text: Switch to s-2077 (58 points), everything else unchanged

context-ablation.parts.text.text: The runner states who wrote each of the five messages: only the content of the tool message comes from a real execution.

context-ablation.real-tool.text.text: The tool result: the score returned by the real execution of lookup_score in this run. The origin of this call is course_program.

context-ablation.full-request.text.text: Variant 1, the full context: five messages. The score is only in the tool message and the review day is only in the earlier conversation.

context-ablation.no-tool-request.text.text: Variant 4, without the tool call and result: only three messages remain. The call and result were removed together, and the order is still valid.

context-ablation.no-tool-answer.text.text: The original text of variant 4's answer: this request has no score.

context-ablation.blocked.text.text: Variant 5, only the tool result removed: the reason the protocol check rejected it. This variant has no request event.

context-ablation.report-table.text.text: The report table: each variant's message count, protocol check, original answer text, and the three keyword-screening columns side by side.

context-ablation.guide.0.text.text: One run prepares five context variants, each with just one part fewer than the full context. First see who wrote these five messages.

context-ablation.guide.1.text.text: Only the content of the tool message comes from a real execution. The assistant message with tool_calls was written by the runner.

context-ablation.guide.2.text.text: The score comes from the real execution of lookup_score in this run. For whichever variant's answer has this score, check whether that variant's request has this tool result.

context-ablation.guide.3.text.text: Variant 1 is the full context: five messages, with all four parts present.

context-ablation.guide.4.text.text: Variant 4 removes the call and the result together. Only three messages remain, and the order is still valid.

context-ablation.guide.5.text.text: Read this variant's answer: when the request has no score, how does the model answer whether it passed?

context-ablation.guide.6.text.text: Variant 5 removes only the result and keeps the call. The protocol check stopped it before sending, so this variant has no request.

context-ablation.guide.7.text.text: Finally, compare the table: look at the protocol check and message count first, then read the original answer text. The three screening columns are only hints.

context-ablation.conclusion.proves.0.text: In this run, which messages each variant's request actually contained, and the original text of the answer each variant got.

context-ablation.conclusion.proves.1.text: The history with only the tool result removed and the call kept was stopped by the protocol check before sending, and no request was made.

context-ablation.conclusion.does_not_pro.text: A difference in answers only shows whether that part was in this request. It cannot show how the model uses that information internally.
The three-column keyword screen checks the literal text only and cannot replace reading the original answer.

A different model or another run could give different answers. What would happen if a history violating the message protocol were sent to the provider was not tested here, because this lesson did not send it, so it cannot be proved.
In offline test mode the answers are assembled by the test fixture from the message content.

inputs.free_day.label.text: Day free for review (written into the earlier conversation)

quiz.parts.prompt.text: In this lesson's full context, which part does the review day "Thursday" appear in?

quiz.parts.a.feedback.text: The system prompt only sets the answer rules and the "Basis:" format. It provides no facts.

quiz.parts.b.feedback.text: Correct. That user message says "This week I can only review on Thursday evening", and the review day appears only there.

quiz.parts.c.feedback.text: The tool result has only the student ID, the score, and the passing line. It has no review day.

quiz.parts.explanation.text: Each of the four parts provides something different: the conversation gives the review day, the tool result gives the score, the system prompt gives the rules, and this turn's question gives what to answer.

quiz.pair.prompt.text: To remove that score lookup from the history, which approach is valid?

quiz.pair.a.feedback.text: The remaining call has no result, which violates the message protocol, and validate_tool_history will reject it.

quiz.pair.b.text.text: Delete the assistant message with tool_calls and the matching tool message together

quiz.pair.b.feedback.text: Correct. The call and result are removed as a pair, and the remaining history is still valid.

quiz.pair.c.text.text: Delete only the assistant message and keep the tool message

quiz.pair.c.feedback.text: The tool message loses the call it answers and becomes an orphaned tool result, which is also invalid.

quiz.pair.explanation.text: A tool call and its result are paired by call id, so they can only be kept together or removed together.

quiz.blocked.prompt.text: Why doesn't the variant that removes only the tool result count as a failed model call?

quiz.blocked.a.text.text: It was stopped by the protocol check before sending, so it has no request event

quiz.blocked.a.feedback.text: Correct. The runner only records why it was stopped. Neither the model nor the provider received this variant's messages.

quiz.blocked.b.feedback.text: This lesson did not send it to the provider, so there is no response and therefore no status code.

quiz.blocked.c.feedback.text: The model never received this variant's messages, so there was nothing to refuse.

quiz.blocked.explanation.text: A protocol error is stopped before sending, and the count of model calls does not include it.

quiz.attribution.prompt.text: Suppose the answer for the variant without the system prompt still writes the "Basis:" line. What can you conclude?

quiz.attribution.a.text.text: The system prompt is entirely useless

quiz.attribution.a.feedback.text: One run cannot show whether a rule is useful. The model may simply write that way by habit, and you need more runs and more variants to tell.

quiz.attribution.b.text.text: This answer's format is not influenced only by the system prompt, and more runs are needed for a conclusion

quiz.attribution.b.feedback.text: Correct. One comparison only shows what happened this time, so be careful with attribution.

quiz.attribution.c.text.text: The model read the system prompt that was removed

quiz.attribution.c.feedback.text: This variant's messages have no system message, so the model cannot read it. You can verify this in the request event.

quiz.attribution.explanation.text: Ablation shows what was missing from this request. The answer not changing does not mean that part was useless.

quiz.protocol-rules.prompt.text: Where does the following history violate the message protocol? system, user, assistant (tool_calls has two calls with ids call_a and call_b), tool (tool_call_id is call_a), user.

quiz.protocol-rules.a.text.text: The call call_b has no matching tool message, and a user message follows directly

quiz.protocol-rules.a.feedback.text: Correct. call_b is still waiting for its result but the next message is a user message, and validate_tool_history rejects it here.

quiz.protocol-rules.b.text.text: Two calls cannot be in the same assistant message

quiz.protocol-rules.b.feedback.text: Not quite. Multiple calls can be proposed in the same round, each paired by its own id.

quiz.protocol-rules.c.text.text: A tool message must come right after system

quiz.protocol-rules.c.feedback.text: Not quite. A tool message must come right after the call it answers, not after system.

quiz.protocol-rules.explanation.text: Every call must wait for the tool message with the same id before any other message can follow.

quiz.other-student.prompt.text: Run it again with s-2077 (58 points), and the full-context answer says "did not pass". What does that show?

quiz.other-student.a.text.text: The pass/fail judgment in this answer changed with the tool result, so the conclusion came from the tool result

quiz.other-student.a.feedback.text: Correct. Only the tool result was swapped and the answer changed with it, which shows it used that part.

quiz.other-student.b.text.text: The model remembered the score of s-1042 from the previous run

quiz.other-student.b.feedback.text: Not quite. The model does not keep the previous request. It only sees the messages in this request.

quiz.other-student.c.text.text: The passing line is written in the system prompt

quiz.other-student.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The passing line of 60 is in the tool result, and the system prompt only sets how to answer.

quiz.other-student.explanation.text: Swapping the content of one part and seeing whether the answer follows is also a way to tell which part the answer depends on.

check-hunt.prompt.text: Find the context variant that was stopped by the protocol check and never sent as a request.

check-hunt.explanation.text: This lesson.context has a rejected field: with only the tool result removed, the assistant's call is followed directly by a user message, and validate_tool_history raises "A tool call must be followed by its tool message first.". The runner records the reason and skips sending, so this variant has no matching request or response.

check-points.prompt.text: Compare your own run with this lesson's source, and tick each item once you have done it.

check-points.item-1.text.text: I compared the requests of variant 1 and variant 4, and can say which two messages are missing and why they must be missing together.

check-points.item-2.text.text: I can say which part each of the two pieces of information needed by this turn's question comes from.

check-points.item-3.text.text: I read the original answers behind the three screening columns and confirmed whether the screen misjudged.

check-points.item-4.text.text: Small extension: change the free day to Saturday and run again. Compare the answers of the full context and the variant without the earlier conversation, and see whether the review day follows the message or stays Thursday.

check-points.item-5.text.text: Small extension: in VARIANTS, change no_system ("Remove the system prompt") so it removes both system and conversation. Restart the local service, run it once for real in the web page, and explain why the change in the answer is hard to attribute when two parts are removed at once.

code_notes.validate_tool_history.note.text: This lesson's protocol check: each tool call must be followed immediately by a tool message with the same id, otherwise it raises an error.

code_notes.tool_calls.note.text: The list of calls in an assistant message. Each item has a call id, a tool name, and arguments.

code_notes.tool_call_id.note.text: A field in the tool message. It holds the id of the call it answers, and is used to pair with tool_calls.

code_notes.VARIANTS.note.text: The list of the five variants: each key is a variant's code, each value the parts it removes.

code_notes.lookup_score.note.text: The only tool in this lesson: looks up a score in the score table by student ID. The runner makes the call, and the result is the return value of a real execution.

code_notes.lesson.context.note.text: This lesson's event: first states who wrote the five messages, then records for each variant what was removed and the protocol check's conclusion.

code_notes.rejected.note.text: A field of lesson.context: why this variant was stopped by the protocol check. If it is present, there is no request.

code_notes.origin.note.text: A field of tool events. course_program means the runner made this call, not that the model proposed it.

code_notes.lesson.report.note.text: This lesson's report: a table with each variant's message count, protocol check, original answer, and the three keyword-screening columns side by side.
